title: Stack & queue problem practice
overview: A practice module with no new code: you use the stack and queue you already built to solve judge problems. The goal is to recognise when a problem is secretly a stack problem (matching, undo, most-recent-first) or a queue problem (first come, first served, rotating order). Solve the linked problems, then check the patterns below.

concepts.explain: A stack only lets you touch the top. Use it when the newest item must be handled first, like the last opened bracket or the last typed character.
Push every opening bracket. On a closing bracket, the top must be its partner; if the stack is empty or the top does not match, the string is invalid. At the end the stack must be empty.
For problems like 'backspace' or 'remove adjacent duplicates', push characters and pop when the new character cancels the top. What is left in the stack is the final string (read it bottom to top).

Pouring a queue into a stack and back reverses it, because the stack gives items back in the opposite order. To reverse only the first k items, pour k items through a stack, then rotate the remaining n-k items to the back.

concepts.term: Inserting at the bottom of a stack
concepts.explain: You cannot reach the bottom directly. Pop everything into a helper (another stack or recursion), push the new value, then push everything back.
Keep a second stack that stores the minimum so far at every level. Push `min(x, minStack.top())` together with each push, and pop both together, so `getMin` is O(1).
A queue adds at the back and removes at the front. Use it when order of arrival matters, or to rotate items (pop from front, push to back).

practice_links.name: Insert An Element At Its Bottom In A Given Stack
Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String
Reverse First K Elements of Queue

recap: Newest-first or 'cancel the last thing' problems are stack problems.
Arrival-order or rotation problems are queue problems.
A stack reverses order; use that to reverse a queue or part of it.
A second stack of running minimums gives O(1) `getMin`.

check_yourself.q: For the string `([)]`, at which character does the bracket check fail, and why?
check_yourself.a: At `)`: the top of the stack is `[`, which is not the partner of `)`.

check_yourself.q: Why is a string like `((` invalid even though no mismatch happens?
check_yourself.a: Because the stack is not empty at the end; two brackets were never closed.

check_yourself.q: You push 5, 3, 7 into a min stack. What does the helper stack hold, bottom to top?
check_yourself.a: 5, 3, 3 — each level stores the smallest value seen so far.

check_yourself.q: How do you reverse only the first k items of a queue of size n?
check_yourself.a: Pop k items into a stack, push them back into the queue (now reversed at the back), then move the front n-k items to the back once each.
